assumptions: a container or equivalent isolation to run a target repository's test suite without trusting it — the security-relevant part, and the one the page does not describe
repository write credentials scoped to open PRs but not to merge, which is a policy decision as much as a configuration one
a real scanner or rule set (Semgrep/CodeQL/GoSec class) rather than "ask the model what looks insecure" — otherwise the eval question is unanswerable
a retry budget plus a distinct FAILED/UNVERIFIED outcome, so an exhausted loop is visible rather than absent
value.why: the demo-able shell (webhook, one model call, one test command, one PR) is a weekend, and that is exactly why the genre is crowded. What is not a weekend: a detector worth trusting for write access, a sandbox that is isolated enough to run untrusted repo tests safely, and a bounded retry policy with a terminal failure state a human can act on.

data_and_models.value: No model is trained here: one model call site family (Gemini 3.5 via google-genai) for reasoning and patch generation, sequenced by ADK, with Firestore for audit-log and state persistence. The load-bearing external dependency is the detector — how a flaw is found in the first place is never stated (no scanner is named in the build prose, and the `owasp` tag is a reference frame, not a component) — so the system's ceiling is set by a component the page does not describe.

how_it_works.value: Three layers, per the page. An AI engine on Gemini 3.5 through the official google-genai SDK, used for code reasoning and patch generation. An agent framework on Google's ADK (Agent Development Kit) to sequence the multi-step reasoning and tool calls. Infrastructure on Google Cloud Run for serverless event handling and test execution, with Firestore holding audit logs and pipeline state. The declared tag list is wider than the prose — fastapi, firebase, gemini-api, google-cloud-firestore, google-genai, owasp, python, react, rest-api, tailwind-css, tanstack-router, typescript, vite — which reads as FastAPI at the webhook edge, a React/Vite/Tailwind console with TanStack Router, and OWASP as the reference frame for what counts as a finding rather than as a component.

how_they_tested.value: The page describes unit tests being *run by the product* inside a containerized sandbox as the gate before a pull request is opened, which is a design claim, not evidence about ZeroDay itself: no test suite for the system, no eval set of known-vulnerable repositories, no detection rate or false-positive rate, and no run log. Nothing is reported on how many patches passed, how many exhausted the retry budget, or what a failed run looks like.

limits_they_disclosed.value: One named engineering problem, and it is the right one: the self-healing loop. When a generated patch failed the sandbox unit tests, the runtime stack trace had to be fed back to the model to produce the next attempt, and the stated difficulty was doing that "without causing infinite retry loops" — i.e. a bounded retry budget is load-bearing, though no bound, no count of attempts and no final failure state are published. No product limitation is admitted: nothing about what the detector cannot find.

value.relation: same event, same shape of problem, opposite answer on the trust boundary: Tower checks obligations against live artifacts and keeps UNVERIFIED as a distinct terminal state so it never asserts what it could not see, whereas ZeroDay's agent acts — writes code and opens a PR — with the target project's tests as its only gate. Read together they are the two available designs for "when is an agent allowed to have an opinion".

also an audit-trail-first agent over code and compliance-shaped evidence; that record publishes a repository and this one does not, so the same claims are checkable there and not here — which is the difference between an unverifiable sound-with-caveats row and an unverifiable thin one.

shares the unattended-monitoring-plus-alerting loop over a live external surface, and stops one step earlier: VMS reports and a human acts, ZeroDay patches. The comparison is worth having because the extra automation step is where all of the difficulty lives (isolation, credentials, failure states) and it is the step this page describes least.

what_breaks_first.value: The detector, because it is undescribed. Everything downstream is careful — sandbox, tests, PR — but a patcher's ceiling is what it notices, and the page names two finding classes (SQL injection, exposed API keys) with no scanner, no ruleset and no false-negative story, so a miss is invisible by construction: the pipeline reports nothing and looks healthy. Second is the retry budget: "under 30 seconds" and "without causing infinite retry loops" cannot both be true for a hard patch, so on a real failure the run either times out mid-loop or silently gives up, and neither terminal state is published. Third is the trust surface — an agent with write access to repositories and a chat assistant over its own audit log is an approval target, and nothing on the page says who authorises the PR beyond a human clicking.

what_it_does.value: ZeroDay AI runs as a background agent over repositories. It watches for security flaws — the page names SQL injection and exposed API keys — and when one is detected it reads the surrounding code, writes a patch, executes the project's unit tests inside a containerized sandbox, and only then opens a GitHub pull request, with the run recorded as an audit log. The pipeline is described end to end as hands-off: a raw vulnerability webhook in, a tested pull request out. A chat assistant sits on top of the same state, and the screenshots show a live-scan view, a topology map of the monitored repositories and a Firestore-backed cloud-info panel. Nothing on the page claims it merges anything: the human review boundary is the pull request itself.

what_it_is.value: An agent that reads a security finding, writes the patch, runs the project's tests in a sandbox, and may not open the pull request until they pass.

what_to_steal.value: Make the verification step able to *refuse*: the agent's output is a pull request only after the target project's unit tests pass in a throwaway container, so "the model wrote something plausible" never becomes a state the system can reach. Then steal the honest framing of the loop around it — the page names the retry bound as the hard part instead of describing the loop as always converging, which is the sentence an autonomous-remediation design usually omits. Third, cheap and specific: a local pre-scan (Gemma, client-side, for syntax errors) before paying for a sandbox run is the same trick as checking a claim against a cache before calling the model — cost the cheap filter first, and only escalate what survives it.

zeroday-ai-autonomous-vulnerability-patc.worth_note: The most crowded genre in this corpus — an agent that finds a flaw, writes a patch and opens a pull request — and this entry publishes no repository, no demo and one number with no denominator, so almost none of it can be checked. It earns a row rather than a pile because two decisions on the page are the correct ones for the genre and are named rather than glossed: the pull request is gated on the project's own tests passing inside a sandbox, and the retry loop's real difficulty is stated as *not looping forever*, which is the failure mode that makes an autonomous patcher dangerous. Read it for those two boundaries; do not read the 30 seconds as a result.
